The mayor versus the minister

By: Joy Summers | Production

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
A battle is brewing between the mayor of Cape Town and the minister of Energy. Stand by to see how your city will be affected

Summary:
The mayor versus the minister

This story began in November 2015 when the City of Cape Town decided they wanted to do things differently. Like all the metro’s Eskom has always supplied their current needs. The city wanted to diversify. With the advent of renewable energy – suddenly they had a choice. now they could get cheaper and cleaner electricity.

The advantages are obvious, renewables are now cheaper per kilowatt hour and the city has a constitutional and statutory duty to find the cleanest and cheapest electricity to provide for its citizens.

This is mandated across a range of legal provisions in the constitution, the local government and municipal systems act and the Electricity regulation act of 2006, so legally the city is on a sound footing. But, there is a catch.

Any Independent power producer who wants to sell its electricity to the city has to be licensed by Nersa to do that. In itself that shouldn’t be an obstacle. But section 34 of the electricity Regulation act vests a range of powers in the minister of Energy, and Nersa would not give the go- ahead to the city, until the minister said so.



Further information:
Nersa believes that an independent power producer may not establish and operate new generation capacity without a ministerial determination in terms of section 34. That presented a problem – no independent power producer will invest in the creation and operation of new generation capacity in the knowledge that NERSA will refuse any application for a license to do so if it is not underpinned by a ministerial determination in terms of section 34.

The city sought a legal opinion from Wim Trengrove SC – his opinion suggested that in fact the city does not need permission from the minister, but if Nersa wont grant licenses without the minister’s go ahead, that left the city in a bind.

So, the city waited. They sent letters, they begged and pleaded for answers from
the former minister of Energy Tina Joemat Peterson, and later her replacement Minister Kubayi.

By July this year mayor Patricia De Lille, had had enough and sought relief from the courts. She has for an order declaring that a ministerial determination in terms of section 34 be set aside.

Even if the courts hold that a ministerial determination is required, then the city asks for an order declaring section 34 unconstitutional and invalid because it unduly interferes with the city’s right and duty to provide electricity to its inhabitants in such a manner as it deems best.

And even if the courts don’t agree with the city then they have asked that the minister be compelled to make a decision within one month. It’s clear according to sources within the city, that they intend to fight this all the way to the constitutional court.

And this battle could be a game changer for ESKOM. The utility is R350 billion rand in debt and that is expected to rise to R500 billion rand; its management is accused of billions of rands funneled illegally to Gupta linked companies, and now they want at another 20% increase next year from its cash strapped customers.

Many municipalities want to follow in the Cape Town’s footsteps, and are carefully watching this case. The Ekurheleni Metropolitan council has already commenced its own process of independent RE generation in order to attain a target of 10% RE energy supply. In effect, the EMC is trying to do the same as the City of Cape Town, namely to get its energy from IPP’s. However, it is approaching it the other way around, by first securing the IPP’s before satisfying regulatory requirements.

This battle will only intensify as Nelson Mandela Bay Metro, Mangaung, Richards Bay and Kwadukuza ( Ballito area) and eThekwini Metro are also exploring their options. But they are all watching what happens in this fight between the City of Cape Town and NERSA and the minister.

THE MINISTER’S RESPONSE
In reply to Carte Blanche at a recent press conference on this matter, the minister accused the mayor of acting prematurely.


Carte Blanche goes to the main players to find out who is winning in a fight that could lead to cheaper and cleaner electricity and mass migration away from Eskom. But that in itself could have serious consequences for the sovereign that stands guarantee for Eskom and is relying on increased revenue just to keep the utility going.

Press Release:


Mayor vs Minister
For two years Mayor Patricia de Lille has been trying to do what she is lawfully obliged to do –
provide the cheapest, cleanest electricity to Cape Town residents. She’s approached two
Ministers and Nersa but none will give her permission to buy electricity directly from independent
power producers, thereby cutting out Eskom. In desperation the Mayor has now gone to court and
the City says it will go all the way to the Constitutional Court if it has to. Could this be a game
changer if the City wins its case?

Script:


Mayor vs minister final script

Commentary One
When Simon Haw looks across the Cape Town city skyline, he sees more than just rooftops

Simon
Every rooftop I look at I see as an opportunity

Commentary Two
So far his company has covered the top of 16 buildings with 10 MW of solar power, that could power around 3000 homes – but he hopes in time, it could be a lot more

Simon Haw
Most of our systems designed to 30 – 40 %
Could do more but we can’t sell the energy back
John
Frustration for you
Simon
Absolutely

Commentary Three
This is the energy revolution that is quietly taking place across our cities. But the rise of rooftop solar is creating trouble for Eskom says a new international report. Eskom needs to pay for Medupi and Kusile, combined estimated cost: R448 billion rand. The last thing it needs is competition from cheaper renewables. What it needs now is revenue, and Eskom has just asked the energy regulator, NERSA, for a 20% increase from next year

MARK
There is something called the utility death spiral

Commentary Four
The utility death spiral is not unique to Eskom. Mark Pickering, chairman of the South African Wind Energy Association, is one of several energy experts now using the term to describe Eskom’s future

Mark
As tariffs rise consumers opt to self -provide, put solar panels on their roof, and as they leave the utility…. has less demand, but to cover its costs it has to put its tariffs up further, leading to more consumers leaving the grid. This utility death spiral is exactly what Eskom has entered – it is an inevitable process and will lead to a crash on Eskom’s part at some point

Commentary five
Against this background, the City of Cape Town has set itself a target. It wants 20% of its energy needs to come from renewables in just three years from now. Leading the charge is mayor Patricia De Lille

PATRICIA
I said we must not be just distributors of electricity – we must generate our own energy!

LINK
Two years ago, the mayor decided it was time to do things differently. The city would buy some of their energy needs directly from independent renewable suppliers, thereby cutting out Eskom. But that has proved to be more difficult than she could have imagined

Commentary Six
The mayor says there is a raft of legislation that compels her to provide the city’s residents with the cheapest cleanest energy. Renewables fit that bill.

Up sound Mayor
We believe that we have an obligation in terms of our constitution that we must provide the best service to our citizens, and at the best price, and what we are being prevented from doing, by the incompetency of our national government, is to exercise our statutory obligations in terms of the constitution

Commentary Seven
At 400 MW, that is only about 20% of the city’s needs. But section 34 of the Electricity act could scupper the mayor’s plans. To cut out Eskom, the city may need permission from the energy minister and NERSA. So, in 2015 she sent off a letter to minister Joemat- Peterson

Patricia
and I said to the minister we would like her to use section 34 in the ACT where she needs to consult with NERSA to give us permission to buy renewable energy directly from IPPS

Commentary eight
But then she waited for feedback. And waited. She sent more letters

Patricia
She absolutely failed. She didn’t consult with NERSA, they never came back to us
John
We understand that things don’t happen quickly in government but sometimes you have to draw a line in the sand don’t you?
Patricia
You have too, I mean, first of all, they want to send a team of technical people to Cape Town to hear what we want to talk to the minister about, and they come on a Friday afternoon to do shopping at the waterfront for the rest of the weekend, then they must go brief the minister before the minister can actually meet with us, that took two years.

Commentary nine
Eventually Minister Joemat-Peteson told the mayor she would make a final decision in March this year

Patricia
before we get to March 2017 she was gone

Commentary ten
The mayor began again with new energy minister Mmamoloko Kubayi. She says that went nowhere

Patricia
she is part of the old clique, the old clique and the old cabinet, together with the old president, they all want to protect Eskom

Commentary eleven
The mayor also asked Wim Trengove SC, for a legal opinion. He advised that the city does not require ministerial determination. However, NERSA refuses to grant licenses to the IPP’s unless the minister gives the go ahead, and the IPP’s won’t invest unless they get licenses from NERSA. Nersa has declined to comment.

LINK
Eventually the mayor ran out of patience and after two years of waiting approached the courts for a solution

PATRICIA
We now said to the court we want a declaratory order. The court must say that section 34 is unconstitutional. That as a local government sphere we are entitled in terms of the constitution to buy and procure anything we need for our citizens

Commentary twelve
At her recent press conference, we canvassed the minister’s view on the mayor’s court application

Minister Kubayi
My objection is to say that it is premature to be in court, I have not dealt with the content of the case itself. I am saying Mayor De Lille should have allowed intergovernmental relations to happen so we could find solutions.

Commentary Thirteen
In September, the minister filed her answering affidavit

John
Madam mayor, we asked the minister Kubayi about your court action and she said you are being premature
Patricia
I don’t care, that is why we have turned to the courts. I mean what is a hurry? What does she mean two years we wrote to them in 2015, 2016, 2017, how could that be a rush? If that is the way they do business in ANC run government departments certainly in CT we don’t work like this




Commentary fourteen
At the city of Ekurhuleni they are watching the Cape Town matter with interest. Mark Wilson is head of the department, Energy

Mark Wilson
We are taking note of what is happening in the city of CT but we are going in our own direction

Commentary fifteen
They began with this small solar experiment next to Watville several years ago. Now the plan is to roll out about 27 PV plants in partnership with power producers for 20 years, who will provide exclusively to the metro

Mark
This will be cheaper than Eskom across the board of all the technologies

Commentary sixteen
And that will mean Eskom will lose a substantial portion of the revenue it currently gets from Ekurhuleni

Mark
I am not sure if Eskom aware of it yet but it will be a massive change to them in terms of loss of income

Commentary Seventeen
But the renewable program has its detractors, and Cosatu don’t trust what the City of Cape Town is trying to do. Previously, they’ve called for the suspension of the governments Renewable energy programme. General Secretary Bheki Ntshalintshali

Beki
In principle we will support such a things, if anybody will say we are going to create jobs, make it cleaner and make it cheaper but there is no evidence that clean energy is cheaper

Commentary eighteen
The cost of renewables, versus coal, is hotly contested, but the mayor believes she can save the city money

Mark
It’s a simple matter of economics. Eskom is charging 90 something cents to municipalities and is proposing a 28% increase at least – the cost of electricity to a municipality like CT is going through the roof – if there are renewable that are prepared to sell to CT at a lower price why should it not choose that

Commentary Seventeen
But in the ministers answering affidavit filed recently, she says that oversupply of electricity will result in power being more expensive.

John
Why level of confusion from government to what the city should do for its citizens
Patricia
Absolutely no confusion! They want to keep the monopoly of Eskom, and we can all see how the state and ministers and board and everyone just looting the SOE’S, so its not in their interests, to allow municipalities to buy and procure their own electricity

Commentary Eighteen
But Cosatu’s concerned about its members losing their jobs when Eskom shuts down its old power stations

Beki
We need it to be suspended so that you can set it up the price correct and do the reskilling of the workers. Those jobs that will disappear because of the introduction of the IPP, must be created somewhere else.

Commentary Nineteen
As the mayor takes on both the minister and NERSA, other metro’s will be watching closely.

John
If your court action is successful and you get what you are hoping for, do you think it will be a game changer
Patricia
It’s going to change it completely

Commentary Twenty
And not for the better for Eskom, because the mayor intends taking this to the highest court in the land
Patricia
And this is where we will end up with this one – we will take it right up to the constitutional
John
You are prepared to take it that far
Patricia
Yes definitely!


THE END 10 03









PROMO ONE
Commentary
Mayor Patricia De Lille has asked the courts for a ruling so that the city of Cape Town can buy power from the Independent power producers, thereby cutting out Eskom

PROMO TWO
Patricia De Lille
I said we must not be just distributors of electricity – we must generate our own energy!
Commentary
Mayor of the city of Cape town wants to buy energy direct from renewable suppliers. But that’s been far more difficult than she could have imagined

PROMO THREE
Minister Kubayi
My objection is to say its premature to be in court
premature
Patricia
What does she mean two years ….

metadata.Summary: The mayor versus the minister This story began in November 2015 when the City of Cape Town decided they wanted to do things differently. Like all the metro’s Eskom has always supplied their current needs. The city wanted to diversify. With the advent of renewable energy – suddenly they had a choice. now they could get cheaper and cleaner electricity. The advantages are obvious, renewables are now cheaper per kilowatt hour and the city has a constitutional and statutory duty to find the cleanest and cheapest electricity to provide for its citizens. This is mandated across a range of legal provisions in the constitution, the local government and municipal systems act and the Electricity regulation act of 2006, so legally the city is on a sound footing. But, there is a catch. Any Independent power producer who wants to sell its electricity to the city has to be licensed by Nersa to do that. In itself that shouldn’t be an obstacle. But section 34 of the electricity Regulation act vests a range of powers in the minister of Energy, and Nersa would not give the go- ahead to the city, until the minister said so.
metadata.Further information: Nersa believes that an independent power producer may not establish and operate new generation capacity without a ministerial determination in terms of section 34. That presented a problem – no independent power producer will invest in the creation and operation of new generation capacity in the knowledge that NERSA will refuse any application for a license to do so if it is not underpinned by a ministerial determination in terms of section 34. The city sought a legal opinion from Wim Trengrove SC – his opinion suggested that in fact the city does not need permission from the minister, but if Nersa wont grant licenses without the minister’s go ahead, that left the city in a bind. So, the city waited. They sent letters, they begged and pleaded for answers from the former minister of Energy Tina Joemat Peterson, and later her replacement Minister Kubayi. By July this year mayor Patricia De Lille, had had enough and sought relief from the courts. She has for an order declaring that a ministerial determination in terms of section 34 be set aside. Even if the courts hold that a ministerial determination is required, then the city asks for an order declaring section 34 unconstitutional and invalid because it unduly interferes with the city’s right and duty to provide electricity to its inhabitants in such a manner as it deems best. And even if the courts don’t agree with the city then they have asked that the minister be compelled to make a decision within one month. It’s clear according to sources within the city, that they intend to fight this all the way to the constitutional court. And this battle could be a game changer for ESKOM. The utility is R350 billion rand in debt and that is expected to rise to R500 billion rand; its management is accused of billions of rands funneled illegally to Gupta linked companies, and now they want at another 20% increase next year from its cash strapped customers. Many municipalities want to follow in the Cape Town’s footsteps, and are carefully watching this case. The Ekurheleni Metropolitan council has already commenced its own process of independent RE generation in order to attain a target of 10% RE energy supply. In effect, the EMC is trying to do the same as the City of Cape Town, namely to get its energy from IPP’s. However, it is approaching it the other way around, by first securing the IPP’s before satisfying regulatory requirements. This battle will only intensify as Nelson Mandela Bay Metro, Mangaung, Richards Bay and Kwadukuza ( Ballito area) and eThekwini Metro are also exploring their options. But they are all watching what happens in this fight between the City of Cape Town and NERSA and the minister. THE MINISTER’S RESPONSE In reply to Carte Blanche at a recent press conference on this matter, the minister accused the mayor of acting prematurely. Carte Blanche goes to the main players to find out who is winning in a fight that could lead to cheaper and cleaner electricity and mass migration away from Eskom. But that in itself could have serious consequences for the sovereign that stands guarantee for Eskom and is relying on increased revenue just to keep the utility going.
